job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Priority issues for Thursday:** items 1, 5, 9, 16, and 21 are the most consequential. They involve internal contradictions, a timing gap, the grandfather clause, and a registry with no penalties.

**Section 2 (Definitions)**

1. **§7(a) and §7(b) conflict.** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in force indefinitely until Congress passes a joint resolution, but §7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment, so the prohibition lapses on schedule regardless of the National Academies process. Drafters need to decide which governs and conform the two.

2. **§2(1)(A) "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator could split a fleet into several vessels that each stay below it. The threshold should be measured per operator, licensee, or project.

3. **§2(1)(A) "per year," "recovery," and "metric tons."** The measurement point is unspecified (wet or dry weight, tonnage at the surface, or tonnage after processing), which gives operators room to argue their volumes fall under the threshold.

4. **§2(1)(A) "mineral resources" and "seabed."** It is unclear whether the term covers sand, gravel, or aggregate, and the 200-meter depth threshold doesn't say how depth is measured or where. Operations just outside those parameters would fall outside the definition.

5. **§2(1)(B) "the Secretary" and "comparable."** The Act never identifies which Secretary is meant (§6 uses "Secretary of State," which invites confusion). The provision also gives open-ended discretion with no standard for "comparable," no notice procedure, and no review standard, inviting both arbitrary-and-capricious and nondelegation challenges.

6. **§2(2) "U.S. person" and "State."** The definition excludes LLCs, partnerships, and other unincorporated entities, which could take a mining operation outside §3(a)'s extraterritorial reach. "State" is also undefined, so it is unclear whether D.C. and the territories are included.

7. **§2(3) "covered vessel."** The 5,000-gross-ton line means a smaller vessel capable of commercial-scale recovery would escape registration. "Equipped for recovery" is undefined and easy to design around, and the tonnage measurement convention isn't specified.

8. **Missing definitions and no findings section.** "Person," "operator," "exploration license," "seabed," and "mineral resources" are undefined, and the Act has no purpose or findings section to guide interpretation. Courts would have to fill these gaps, and the outcome might not match what the sponsors intend.

**Section 3 (Prohibition and exceptions)**

9. **§3(b) grandfather clause.** It protects any mining "conducted under an exploration license issued before" enactment, with no time limit, no volume cap, and no requirement that the license be unexpired. A license renewed or extended indefinitely could shield commercial-scale recovery, and "under an exploration license" could be read to cover commercial recovery nominally conducted under an exploration authorization.

10. **§3(a) and §3(b): interaction with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (1980).** That statute, administered by NOAA, authorizes licenses and permits for U.S. citizens to mine the international seabed. The bill doesn't mention, repeal, or preserve it, and §3(b) covers only "exploration license[s]," so it's unclear whether commercial recovery permits or pending applications are affected. Staff should confirm the current status of any DSHMRA authorizations before the markup.

11. **§3(a) "engage in" is undefined.** The prohibition may not reach financing, insurance, equipment supply, chartering, or contracting for foreign deep-seabed mining, so a U.S. company could support such operations without violating the Act.

12. **§3(a) has no import or sales restriction.** Minerals recovered abroad could still be imported, processed, and sold in the United States, which undercuts the Act's purpose.

13. **§3(a) "in the United States" and "anywhere."** It's unclear whether "in the United States" covers the exclusive economic zone and continental shelf, where the U.S. exercises jurisdiction over seabed resources. The Act also doesn't address U.S.-flagged vessels operating in areas beyond national jurisdiction, and "person" is undefined (the Dictionary Act may fill that gap, but explicit language is better).

14. **§3(c) "environmental assessment."** The Act doesn't define the purpose, cap tonnage, duration, or area, or require registration or agency authorization. This is an easy pretext for commercial-scale recovery, and "purpose" is difficult to prove or disprove.

**Section 4 (Registry)**

15. **§4(a) "operator" is undefined.** It's unclear whether the operator is the owner, charterer, or manager, and a company could argue that no single party is the "operator" required to register.

16. **§4 has no penalties.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false certification carries no penalty under this Act. As drafted, the registry is effectively voluntary.

17. **§4(b) reporting duty is circular.** The reporting obligation applies only to a "registered operator," so an operator who never registers has no reporting duty at all.

18. **§4(b) report content and deadlines are undefined.** The Act doesn't specify tonnage, location, depth, or environmental monitoring data, and "describing recovery activities" is too vague to enforce §2(1)(A). There is no filing deadline, no public disclosure requirement, and no duty on NOAA to review the reports.

19. **§4 lacks implementing authority.** NOAA isn't given rulemaking power to set forms, define terms, or establish procedures, and no funding is provided.

**Section 5 (Penalties)**

20. **§5(a) "per day" is ambiguous.** The Act doesn't say whether violations are counted per day, per vessel, or per ton, or how continuing violations are counted. The $1,000,000 figure is a maximum with no factors for courts or agencies to consider, and the Act doesn't say whether it is adjusted for inflation.

21. **§5 has no enforcement mechanism.** The Act names no enforcing agency and gives no investigative or subpoena power, no injunctive authority, no citizen-suit provision, no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals, and no administrative penalty procedure. Enforcing against foreign-flagged vessels would be especially difficult.

22. **§5(b) "willfully" is undefined.** The Act also doesn't say how criminal liability applies to corporate officers or vessel masters.

**Section 6 (International agreement)**

23. **§6 "seek to negotiate" creates no real obligation.** There is no requirement to conclude an agreement, no report to Congress if negotiations fail, and no consequence for the domestic prohibition. The phrase "equivalent to those in section 3" is also unclear, and the section doesn't address the International Seabed Authority, U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea (which the U.S. has not ratified), or whether Senate consent is required.

**Section 7 (Duration)**

24. **§7(a) "serious harm" is undefined.** The joint resolution has no objective standard to apply, so the finding could be contested.

25. **§7(a) doesn't require the National Academies report.** There is no deadline and no requirement that the report be commissioned or produced, and it's unclear whether Congress can act without one. This could stall indefinitely or invite arguments that a resulting resolution is invalid.

26. **§7(a) joint resolution is unclear in effect.** A joint resolution that "finds" something doesn't obviously change statutory law. Drafters should specify whether it repeals or suspends §3, which would also determine whether presentment and the veto apply.

27. **§7(b) has no savings clause.** It's unclear whether violations committed before the sunset, or pending enforcement actions, survive. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) addresses repeals and may not clearly apply when a provision simply "ceases to have effect."

**Section 8 (Effective date) and general drafting**

28. **§8 conflicts with §5(a) and §3(b).** The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment, but §5(a) penalizes violations "on or after the date of enactment," and §3(b) cuts off the grandfather at enactment. This creates a 180-day window in which the prohibition isn't yet effective, which gives operators an incentive to accelerate operations or license issuances.

29. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes the §2(1)(B) delegation or the §7(a) mechanism, the Act doesn't say whether the remaining provisions survive.

---

**Caveats:** This is a drafting and policy review for internal use, not legal advice. Before the markup, staff should confirm with Senate Legislative Counsel or Commerce Committee staff, and verify the current status of any DSHMRA licenses or permits, since I can't check current records.
